cards.title: Inside the box — every part has one clear job
cards.takeaway: Opening a desktop case is like looking under a car bonnet: once you know six main parts, nothing inside looks scary.
cards.body:
When beginners first open a desktop computer, all the wires and chips look complicated. Good news: a computer is simply **a small team of separate parts**, and each part does **one plain job**!

Learn how a city, a brain, a worktable, and a warehouse work together, and you already understand computer hardware.

cards.title: Motherboard (the city) & CPU (the brain)
cards.takeaway: The Motherboard is the big flat board connecting every part together; the CPU is the brain chip that runs instructions.
cards.body:
Meet the first two stars inside the case:
- **Motherboard:** The large flat circuit board bolted inside the case. Think of it as **the city roads** where every other part plugs in and talks to each other.
- **CPU (Processor):** A small square chip clipped onto the motherboard under a cooling fan/heatsink. It is **the brain** that calculates and executes every program instruction.

check.prompt: What are the jobs of the Motherboard and the CPU?

choices.text: Motherboard connects all parts so they can communicate; CPU is the brain that runs instructions
Motherboard displays pictures; CPU stores movies when power is off
Motherboard cools the room; CPU converts wall AC to DC power
Both are used only for playing audio through speakers

check.hint: Remember our analogy: the city roads (Motherboard) vs. the brain (CPU).
check.explanation: Spot on! Every component plugs into the motherboard, and the CPU is the processor chip that carries out instructions.

cards.title: RAM vs. Storage (HDD / SSD) — Worktable vs. Filing Cabinet!
cards.takeaway: RAM is fast short-term memory wiped when power goes off; Storage (SSD or HDD) keeps your files permanently even unplugged.
cards.body:
Beginners mix up **RAM** and **Storage** more than anything else — here is the easiest way to never confuse them again:
- **RAM (Random Access Memory) = Your Desk / Worktable:** Holds the apps and files you have **open right now**. Super fast, **short-term** — when power goes off, the worktable clears!
- **Storage (SSD or Hard Drive) = Your Filing Cabinet / Warehouse:** Keeps your Windows OS, photos, and videos **permanently**, even when unplugged for a year!

*Common mistake:* Adding **more RAM** makes multitasking smoother, **not** more space to store movies! To store more videos, upgrade **Storage (SSD/HDD)**.

check.prompt: A friend says: 'My drive is full, so I will buy more RAM to store more movies.' What is the right correction?

choices.text: They are right — RAM stores movies permanently
RAM is only temporary working memory for open apps; to store more movies permanently, upgrade the SSD or Hard Drive (HDD)
They should replace the cooling fan to gain movie storage
Movies are stored inside the power supply unit

check.explanation: Exactly! RAM clears as soon as power goes off. Permanent files like movies live on your SSD or HDD.

cards.title: Spinning HDD vs. Fast Silent SSD
cards.takeaway: An HDD has spinning metal platters (clicking/ticking = failing drive — back up now!); an SSD has no moving parts and is much faster.
cards.body:
Two types of permanent storage drives exist:
- **HDD (Hard Disk Drive):** Uses spinning magnetic platters inside. Cheaper for big sizes, slower, and fragile if dropped. **Warning sign:** A soft **clicking or ticking sound** plus slow file loading means the spinning HDD is failing — **back up the customer's data immediately** before it dies!
- **SSD (Solid State Drive):** Pure flash chips with **zero moving parts** — silent, shock-resistant, and boots Windows 5× faster!

cards.title: Power Supply Unit (PSU) — and the #1 safety rule!
cards.takeaway: The PSU converts dangerous high-voltage wall power into safe low-voltage DC — NEVER open a PSU casing, even unplugged!
cards.body:
The **PSU (Power Supply Unit)** is the metal box where the wall power cord plugs in. It converts 220–240V AC wall electricity into safe 12V/5V/3.3V DC for computer parts.

**CRITICAL SAFETY RULE:**
**NEVER open the metal casing of a PSU**, even when unplugged! Large capacitors inside hold **deadly high voltage** long after power is disconnected. If a PSU is faulty, replace the whole unit!

check.prompt: Why must a technician NEVER unscrew and open a faulty Power Supply Unit (PSU), even after unplugging it?

choices.text: Opening it deletes files on the SSD
Internal capacitors store dangerous, potentially lethal high voltage even after unplugging
Sunlight ruins the cooling fan blades

check.hint: Capacitors inside a power supply hold high electrical charge long after the wall plug is pulled.
check.explanation: Safety first! PSU capacitors retain lethal voltage even unplugged — technicians replace a faulty PSU whole, never open it.

cards.title: Cooling fans, heatsinks & static safety
cards.takeaway: Before touching inner boards, unplug power and touch unpainted metal on the case to discharge static electricity.
cards.body:
Processors get hot fast, so a metal **heatsink and fan** sit right on top of the CPU with thermal paste.

Whenever you work inside a PC:
1. Shut down and **unplug** the power cable from the back.
2. Touch bare unpainted metal on the case first so static electricity on your fingers cannot zap delicate RAM or motherboard chips.

cards.title: Fans spin, light is ON, screen stays BLACK? Check simple things first!
cards.takeaway: Check monitor power & video cable first, then check which display port is used, then reseat loose RAM sticks.
cards.body:
When a desktop powers on (fans spin) yet the monitor stays black, work from **simplest outside checks to inside**:
1. **Monitor power & input:** Is the monitor turned on and plugged in?
2. **Video cable (HDMI / VGA):** Is it firmly plugged in at both ends — and plugged into the **graphics card** (if installed) rather than the motherboard port?
3. **Reseat RAM:** Unplug power, unclip the RAM stick, and press it firmly back in until the side clips click!

check.prompt: A customer's PC makes a soft ticking sound from a spinning part inside and files open very slowly. What part is failing and what do you do FIRST?

choices.text: The keyboard is dusty — wash the keys
The spinning Hard Disk Drive (HDD) is failing — back up the customer's important files immediately before replacing it with an SSD
The monitor cable is loose — buy a bigger screen
Open the PSU with a screwdriver

check.hint: Only fans and HDDs spin — and slow file opening + ticking points straight to mechanical storage!
check.explanation: Spot on! Ticking + slow file reads is classic mechanical HDD failure. Always back up customer data first before the drive stops spinning altogether!
